title: 7 UX Pilot Alternatives Worth Trying in 2026
summary: UX Pilot alternatives for designers, sorted by how deeply each works with Figma: built in, plugins that draw screens or write code, and paste-in tools.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- UX Pilot now works inside Figma through its Nodey plugin, so the case for switching rests on its plans and terms: export from the web app to Figma starts on Pro at $29 a month, or $19 billed yearly; free designs are non-commercial only; and there are no refunds.
- Of the six tools after ours, only Figma's agent is built into Figma, and two publish a plugin that draws new screens on the canvas the way Nodey does: Anima, through Buddy, and UXMagic.
- MagicPath Builder is the cheapest paid route into Figma here, at $10 a month billed monthly or $7 billed annually, with unlimited Figma exports.
- Locofy and Anima's code plugin sit on the other side of the handoff: they turn frames you've already drawn into front-end code.


We read the UX Pilot alternatives pages that rank today, and none of them mentions UX Pilot 2.0, which shipped in July 2026, or its new Figma plugin, Nodey. Nodey draws native, editable Figma layers from your own components, on the same account and credits as the web app.


So this list is for designers who make hi-fi screens in or next to Figma.[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) comes first because it's our product, and it has no Figma plugin, export or design-system import. After it, each tool sits in its deepest Figma tier: built into Figma, then a plugin that draws new screens, then a plugin that turns frames into code, then tools that export from their own canvas.


Inside a tier, the cheapest paid plan billed monthly goes first. Prices, credits and plan limits below were read from each vendor's site on November 13, 2026.


## Why designers look past UX Pilot


UX Pilot is still independent, still open to signups and still shipping: 2.0 added an MCP server, and it now also runs a GitHub design-review agent and a video product called Motion. The reasons designers look elsewhere sit in its plans, its terms and the trip from its canvas into Figma.


### Export and banked credits need a paid plan


Free gives you 80 credits a day with no rollover, one project and every design feature, but no web-app export to Figma or code. Pro costs $29 billed monthly, or $19 a month billed yearly, for 750 credits a month and up to 125 screens. Teams is $39 a user a month, or $31 billed yearly, for 2 to 15 seats.


Paid credits behave differently. Under UX Pilot's Terms, plan credits roll over and accumulate monthly, but only while your subscription is active, so canceling locks away whatever you've banked until you come back.


### The terms are strict on free work and refunds


UX Pilot's Terms, last updated November 2, 2026, say free plan users "may only use generated designs for personal, non-commercial purposes." So a mockup made on Free can't go into client work. The same Terms rule out refunds, so a month of Pro you don't use is still a month you've paid for.


### A full design system means Enterprise


Every plan can import Figma components, and Nodey reuses them as instances. Importing a full design system and fine-tuning the AI on it is Enterprise only, priced on request and billed annually, and UX Pilot's design-system service says that import is done "typically within three weeks".


### Interactions may not make the trip


In about April 2026, a reply on UX Pilot's own Figma plugin page told a user that "dynamic elements and interactions do not export along with the design when exporting to Figma." A 2025 thread on Reddit's r/UI_Design,[UX Pilot plugin complaints](https://www.reddit.com/r/UI_Design/comments/1l8qfqk/ux_pilot_plugin_is_not_so_good_need_suggestions/) , shows the user's side: the poster liked the designs, but "whatever the navigation we had in UX pilot are lost" in Figma.


A reply added, "I have the exact same issue and have made multiple tickets about this." It's anecdotal and predates 2.0. The plugin-page reply predates 2.0 too and promised a fix, so test one interactive flow yourself before you trust the round trip. If you were also weighing Figma's prompt-to-prototype tool, our[Figma Make alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/figma-make-alternatives) roundup compares those tools.


## The best UX Pilot alternatives, by Figma depth


Our sort order lives in the last column: where does the work happen relative to Figma? Pricing shows any free plan, then the cheapest paid plan billed monthly.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


To keep generating on the canvas, start with the Figma agent, Anima's Buddy or UXMagic; for code from finished frames, start with Anima's code plugin or Locofy.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Screens that need to go live


**Overview:** Awesomic has no Figma plugin, no Figma export and no design-system import, so we can't replace Nodey on your canvas. We replace the step after the mockup, when someone rebuilds the screen as a real page.


Describe the screen, and our agent builds a working page you can click through and publish to a live link. Image models such as Nano Banana, GPT Image and FLUX draw what goes on it, while one memory of your brand, files and decisions keeps screen twelve in line with screen one.


When a screen needs a designer's judgment, our separate All-in-One plan puts a vetted UI/UX designer on it, matched in as little as 24 hours, and you hand over the task from the same chat. Awesomic counts 20,000+ delivered projects.


**Key features:**


- Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode, several at once, each in its own chat.
- A share link for review before anything goes live.
- 200+ templates to start from.
- Free rematches and a dedicated account manager on expert plans.


**Pricing:** You pay per person per month for an Agentic plan, and what you pay becomes that person's monthly AI budget. The four tiers are Light at $19, Basic at $99, Pro at $199 and Studio at $499, all billed monthly and none refundable.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


So a solo designer on Light spends $219 a month before seat fees, by our math. All-in-One lists at $3,219 and already includes one Light subscription, so adding the fee brings it to at least $3,419, again by our math (our Terms are silent on whether that Light carries a fee of its own).


**Pros:** Clickable pages instead of static mockups, brand memory across screens, parallel agents, a UI/UX designer on the separate All-in-One plan


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Choose Light to test the agents, or All-in-One for a designer.
2. Read the checkout total, fee and all, before you pay.
3. Write a sentence or two about the screen, or drop in your brief.
4. Flag what's wrong in the chat and let the agent fix it.
5. Publish it to a live link and send it for review.


**Why it's a good UX Pilot alternative:** The screen you approve is already a working page, one click from a live link, so there's no export-and-rebuild step.


**Final verdict:** If you live in Figma and want generated layers there, the Figma agent or a screen-drawing plugin suits you better. Choose Awesomic when the screen must become a working page, or when a vetted designer should own the result.


[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) and describe the first screen you'd otherwise rebuild by hand.


### 2. Figma agent


**Overview:** If you want generated screens without leaving Figma, start with the agent built into Figma. It replaced First Draft in May 2026 and left beta on October 6, 2026. You open it from the left rail, or select a layer and press Cmd or Ctrl + Enter.


Unlike Nodey, it doesn't sync your system into a second tool: it works with the libraries already connected to your file, so you @-mention real components, variables and styles. Edits need a Full seat with edit access; Collab, Dev and View seats can chat with it, and anyone can use it in their own drafts.


**Key features:**


- Parallel prompts across several frames at once.
- Bulk edits such as renaming variables, swapping components or building a dark mode.
- Code layers, interactive prototypes backed by running code, in open beta on all plans.


**Pricing:** Starter is free, with 150 AI credits a day up to 500 a month, but the agent has only limited availability there. Figma's Professional plan charges $20 a month per Full seat billed monthly, or $16 on annual billing, and that seat adds 3,000 AI credits a month, shared with every other Figma AI feature, Make included.


**Pros:** Nothing extra to install or sync, your own library on the canvas, out of beta


**Cons:** Edits need a Full seat, credits are shared with every Figma AI feature, it won't publish new assets to your shared library on its own


**Why it's a good UX Pilot alternative:** You get generated layers built from your own components without paying a second vendor or managing a second credit pool.


**Final verdict:** Pick the Figma agent if your team already pays for Full seats and keeps its design system in a Figma library.


### 3. Anima


**Overview:** Anima publishes a Figma plugin for each end of the handoff. Buddy, at version 91 since September 28, 2026, is a design agent you chat with: it generates screens, flows, components and variants on the canvas, using your real components, variables and auto layout.


Its code plugin, at version 804 since October 28, 2026, works the other way, turning a frame you've drawn into responsive HTML, React or Vue. From Starter up, the pricing grid lists Figma to code "both ways", so generated code can go back into Figma as you iterate.


Anima also imports design-system components, takes a brand's look from a website address or a Design.md file, and serves coding agents through an MCP server and an API.


**Key features:**


- Screens, flows and components generated on the canvas through Buddy.
- Frame-to-code conversion in HTML, React or Vue, with code copied back into Figma from Starter.
- Design-system component import.


**Pricing:** Free covers 5 chat messages and 5 code generations, and the pricing page doesn't list a price for Buddy. Starter is $25 a seat a month, or $20 billed annually, for 50 code generations and 100 chat messages, and Pro is $50, or $40 billed annually, for 200 code generations.


**Pros:** Generated screens and real code from one vendor, a round trip back into Figma, a free plan you can test the code plugin on


**Cons:** Every plugin export, import, clone or prompt spends a code generation, Starter stops at 50 a month, SSO only on annual Business or Enterprise plans


**Why it covers both ends:** Buddy drafts the screen from your library, and the code plugin turns the finished frame into code for your developers.


**Final verdict:** Choose Anima if you want screens drawn on your canvas and front-end code from the same vendor.


### 4. UXMagic


**Overview:** UXMagic is built the way UX Pilot is, with a generating plugin and a web app on one account. Its Figma plugin, at version 20 since August 21, 2026, generates screens, flows and design systems directly on your canvas from text, a sketch or a screenshot, and the web app exports HTML, React and Tailwind code.


UXMagic imports Figma components or a whole design system, so your library comes along. Flow Mode drafts a multi-screen flow from one prompt, a PRD can seed a design, and exports reach past Figma to Framer, Webflow and Canva.


**Key features:**


- Screen generation on the Figma canvas through the plugin.
- Figma component and design-system import.
- Code export to HTML, React and Tailwind.


**Pricing:** Free gives you 20 credits a day, up to 3 screens daily and a single Figma export. Pro is $35 a month, or $17.50 a month billed annually, with 2,400 monthly credits, up to 400 screens and 250 Figma exports.


**Pros:** Generates on the canvas the way Nodey does, half price on annual billing, Figma layers and code from one account


**Cons:** One Figma export on Free, a 250-export cap on Pro, team seats and a shared design-system library only on custom-priced Enterprise


**How it compares on the canvas:** At $35 billed monthly it costs more than UX Pilot Pro's $29, but annual billing drops it to $17.50, just under UX Pilot's $19.


**Final verdict:** Choose UXMagic if you want Nodey's way of working from a different vendor and can live with an export cap.


### 5. Locofy


**Overview:** Locofy is a design-to-code tool with no screen generator. Its Locofy Lightning plugin, at version 562 since September 24, 2026, converts frames you've already drawn into React, React Native, Angular, Flutter, Next.js or Vue.


Its plans count frames and tokens rather than screens. Hobby converts one frame at a time, with up to 10 frames per project, and Pro raises that to 25. Custom components, the route your own design system takes into the code, sit on Enterprise along with GitHub integration.


**Key features:**


- Figma, Penpot and Adobe XD frames converted to front-end code.
- React, Angular, Next.js and Vue for web builds.
- React Native and Flutter for mobile apps.


**Pricing:** There's no lasting free plan: "Free" is a 7-day trial of Hobby with 2,000 LDMtokens, and it converts to the paid Hobby plan afterward. Hobby is $40 a month and Pro is $80, both billed monthly, because annual billing is only offered on Enterprise.


**Pros:** The widest framework choice in this list, mobile frameworks included, Pro content never used to train or improve the platform


**Cons:** The free tier is a 7-day trial, Hobby content may be used to improve the platform, custom components and GitHub integration only on Enterprise


**Who should shortlist it:** Teams shipping Flutter or React Native apps from Figma, which no other plugin here lists.


**Final verdict:** Choose Locofy if your developers want framework code from finished frames, Flutter and React Native included.


### 6. MagicPath


**Overview:** MagicPath does its work on its own canvas, then hands it to Figma by copy and paste, with no plugin involved. Select a frame, click Copy to Figma and paste, and it lands as editable layers with frames, text, fills, strokes and effects preserved. Its docs don't say whether auto layout or component links survive, so test one frame first.


Traffic runs the other way, too. Copy a selection in Figma, paste it onto the MagicPath canvas, and it becomes React components, with no AI and no credits spent. Since version 2.0, outside agents such as Codex, Claude Code and Cursor can work on the canvas, and designs can be pushed to a repo as React.


**Key features:**


- Unlimited Figma copies on Builder and above.
- Figma selections pasted in as React components.
- Your own design system on every plan.


**Pricing:** Free includes 20 daily credits, capped at 120 a month, plus 3 Figma exports and 5 imports a month. Builder costs $10 a month, or $7 billed annually, and makes Figma exports unlimited with 25 imports a month, while Pro is $30, or $21 billed annually, with a 600-credit pack.


**Pros:** Unlimited Figma exports on Builder, a few Figma exports even on Free, a two-way paste between Figma and code


**Cons:** No plugin, so every move is a manual copy and paste, credit packs reset each billing cycle, moving from annual to monthly means canceling first


**Where it wins on price:** No other paid plan in this list gets your work into Figma for less, on either billing basis.


**Final verdict:** Choose MagicPath if you're happy to design outside Figma and paste the results in.


### 7. Banani


**Overview:** Banani turns a plain-language description of your product into editable, multi-screen prototypes, then sends them to Figma or code. Like MagicPath, it skips the plugin: you copy a generated design and paste it into Figma, where on paid plans it arrives as editable layers with auto layout intact.


The free plan is where it gets confusing. Banani's product page presents Figma export as free, but its pricing FAQ limits Figma export to paid plans, and we'd go by the FAQ. Design-system import sits on Enterprise beside SSO, and every plan includes an MCP server.


**Key features:**


- Multi-screen prototypes from one product description.
- Paste-in Figma layers that keep auto layout, from Plus up.
- HTML and CSS code from any paid plan.


**Pricing:** Free has 12 monthly and 3 daily credits, with no card needed. Plus costs $20 a month, or $12 billed annually, for 100 monthly and 10 daily credits and unlimited Figma export, and Pro is $50, or $30 billed annually, with unlimited credits.


**Pros:** Auto layout survives the paste, unlimited credits on Pro, 40% off with annual billing


**Cons:** No Figma export on Free, a single generation typically costs more than one credit, design-system import only on Enterprise


**Its pull for flow work:** You describe a product once and get several connected screens to finish in Figma.


**Final verdict:** Choose Banani if you start from flows rather than single screens and want auto layout to survive the paste.


## What actually lands in Figma


Prices hide the bigger difference: the form your work takes in Figma. Layers drawn on the canvas come from the Figma agent, Anima's Buddy, UXMagic and UX Pilot's own Nodey. All four build them from components you already have, so a teammate can pick them up with less cleanup.


Pasted frames from MagicPath and Banani arrive as editable layers too, but they were built on another canvas. Code from Locofy and Anima's code plugin is a different output again: the frame stays yours, and the code goes to your developers.


### Design systems are still the hard part


In an April 2026 r/UXDesign thread on Reddit, a contractor asked for a fast way to get[designs from a design system](https://www.reddit.com/r/UXDesign/comments/1sh6c8s/ai_generated_designs_from_figma_design_systems/) . One reply said "Out of the box there is nothing to truly help you" without wiring an AI to read Figma over MCP, and another said results depend on a very well-built system. It's anecdotal, and it predates the agent's general release.


Research pointed at this gap earlier. At DIS '24, an ACM design conference,[Takaffoli, Li and Mäkelä](https://villemakela.me/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/takaffoli-et-al.-2024-genai-in-ux-design-and-research.pdf) interviewed 24 UX practitioners, who favored generative AI for writing tasks and noted its limits for wireframing and prototyping. Participants asked for tools "factoring in the provided design system when generating UIs."


Before you hand any of these tools your library, a[design system audit](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/design-system-audit) tells you whether your components and tokens are clean enough for an AI to reuse.


### Developers check the code that comes out


The code side has its own doubts. In a survey presented at MUM '25,[Irawati, Bolukbasi and Riener](https://d-nb.info/1384547347/34) collected 224 replies, 69 of them from developers. The primary barriers developers cited were the accuracy and reliability of generated code, at 67%, and how well an AI tool would integrate with their existing techniques, at 52%.


The respondents were mainly experienced professionals from corporate and multinational enterprises, so treat the poll as a signal rather than a census, and have a developer review Anima or Locofy output before it ships.


## What a designer pays to get work into Figma


Here's the cheapest plan that does each tool's Figma job on both billing bases, with what it caps and UX Pilot first for reference.


On monthly billing, MagicPath, Banani, the Figma Full seat and Anima's Starter all cost less than UX Pilot's $29, and Locofy's Hobby, at $40, is the priciest Figma route here. On yearly billing, four tools come in under UX Pilot Pro's $19: MagicPath, Banani, Figma's Full seat and UXMagic.


Teams on Full seats already have the Figma row on their bill, and our[Figma pricing guide](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/figma-pricing) breaks down what each seat type includes. Our own row buys no Figma plugin, export or design-system import; its $219 is one person's agent budget plus the fee.


## UX Pilot competitors we left out


Some former UX Pilot competitors are gone or have changed course. When we checked, Musho's and Creatie's domains were for sale and Magician's address redirected to an unrelated site, while Motiff has been discontinued and Codia's pricing page now leads with a slides product, though it still sells Figma plugin plans.


Three live tools came close. Builder.io's Visual Copilot is another frame-to-code plugin, at $30 a user a month, or $24 billed annually, on Pro. Figr exports to Figma even on its free plan. Google Stitch was the third, but our[Google Stitch alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/google-stitch-alternatives) roundup is already built around it.


## How to choose a UX Pilot alternative


Pick among these UX Pilot alternatives by where you want the work to happen, then by price:


- If your library lives in Figma and your team has Full seats, try the Figma agent first.
- If you liked Nodey and want the same plugin workflow from another vendor, try Anima's Buddy or UXMagic.
- If developers need code from finished frames, compare Anima for React, HTML or Vue with Locofy for Flutter, React Native or Angular.
- If budget decides, MagicPath Builder gets unlimited editable frames into Figma for $10 a month.
- If you start from multi-screen flows, try Banani on a paid plan, since Free can't export to Figma.


Whichever you pick, check that components arrive as instances, auto layout holds and links between screens survive. If the gap turns out to be design judgment rather than tooling, start with[hiring a UI designer](https://www.awesomic.com/hire/hire-a-ui-designer) instead of buying another plan.


## Where to start this week


Keep UX Pilot Free while you test, and run the same brief through two tools from different tiers, say the Figma agent and MagicPath. Judge what lands in Figma, not the preview, and time the cleanup.


The winner is the tool whose output needs the least fixing on your own library. For the wider set of tools designers keep beside Figma, our[UI design tools](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/ui-design-tools) guide is a good next read.


## FAQ


### Does UX Pilot work inside Figma now?


Yes. Its Figma plugin, now called Nodey, is free to install and generates native, editable Figma layers, reusing your components as instances through a feature it calls Simple Sync. It shares your account and credit balance with the web app. Exporting designs from the web app into Figma is a separate feature, and that one needs Pro or above.


### Is Figma's AI agent still in beta?


No. Figma moved its agent out of beta on October 6, 2026, and its May announcement said AI credits would apply from general availability. Full seats on paid plans can edit with it, other seats can chat with it, and Starter has limited availability.


### Which UX Pilot alternative works best with an existing design system?


The Figma agent, because it uses the libraries already connected to your file: components, variables and styles. MagicPath lets you use your own design system on every plan, Anima and UXMagic import design-system components, and UXMagic keeps a shared team library for Enterprise. On UX Pilot, Banani and Locofy, full design-system support is Enterprise only.


### Can I use UX Pilot's free designs for client work?


No. UX Pilot's Terms, updated November 2, 2026, limit designs made on the Free plan to personal, non-commercial use, and the same Terms rule out refunds. If a design is going to a client, budget for the Pro plan, $19 a month on yearly billing or $29 month to month.


### I'm not a designer. Which of these should I use?


Probably none of them, because this list assumes you already work in Figma. If you want quick wireframes or mockups from a screenshot or a plain description, our[Visily alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/visily-alternatives) roundup is written for that job.
